Read-only research task. File to search: /private/tmp/live-spec-roadmap-wave/wt-baseline/skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md (708 lines).

Context: this is a live-spec "pack" project. A chat-law hook at ~/.claude/hooks/chat-law-hook.sh states seven short "chat laws" for how the AI session must act. I need to find every place in this SKILL.md file where the FULL TEXT of one of these seven laws is STATED (verbatim or as a paraphrase that conveys the actual rule content) — not just a name, number, or one-line pointer reference to it elsewhere. A bare mention like "see rule 5" or a label with no explanatory content does NOT count; a paragraph that explains what the rule requires DOES count, even if terse.

The seven laws, with their short names and their "Home" citations from the hook (use these citations to find candidate base rules by number: rule 2, rule 5, rule 25, rule 29 are named explicitly as homes for some laws):

1. answer-first — open every reply with the outcome/answer first, detail after. (Home: personal profile only, likely NOT restated here, but check.)
2. plain-words-narrate — use plain product words with the human; internal codes/project-coined metaphors may only trail in parentheses at end of line; narrate progress while working (write a line on each pipeline step pass/discovery/plan change, naming the wish and pipeline step; digest after finished step; ~10min heartbeat if nothing to report). Home: "base rule 2 (SPEC INV-28)" for plain words, and "the narration law (SPEC INV-35)" for narration — SPEC INV-35 lives in the profile per other doc, but check if rule 2 area also covers narration.
3. industry-words-register-lint — in chat use standard industry words in the chat language, never render pack-internal English terms word for word (no calques); before showing any artifact/rendered page/mockup/decision page/report, run scripts/preshow-register-lint.py <path>, non-zero exit blocks showing. Home: personal profile + "register-lint law (SPEC INV-83)".
4. no-contrast-frame — name each thing by its own positive sentence; ban "X, not Y" / "X — не Y" contrast-frame constructions in chat, docs, artifacts, product copy, worker briefs; a plain prohibition alone is fine. Home: personal profile only — check if restated here anyway.
5. routing — orchestrator seat (this session) plans/briefs/accepts; workers execute. Unit carrying a decision/design choice -> opus; multi-step mechanical unit -> sonnet; single step -> haiku; size of unit (text/files touched) never changes tier. Workers locate their own anchors (files/lines). A long read ending in a verdict/decision stays with orchestrator; a read done only to understand is dispatched to a reader worker, orchestrator reads only the summary. Home: "base rule 5 for the routing (SPEC INV-69), and base rule 25 for the reading discipline (SPEC INV-137)" — THIS ONE SHOULD BE HERE, likely rule 5 and rule 25 sections.
6. deferral-retest — before parking an item for the human or opening AskUserQuestion, re-test by derivability: does a written source already answer it (base rule, PRODUCT_SPEC.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, approved prototype, past decision)? If yes, act on it, cite source, drop marker. Park only for taste/policy/irreversible act/real device, name which. Irreversible = state before it can't be recovered without loss (spending money, deleting data, unrecallable send); a push to project's own repo reverts so stays with session. A marker/question naming none of the four is itself a finding; item defaults to session. Home: "base rule 29 (SPEC INV-152)". THIS SHOULD BE HERE as rule 29.
7. root-naming — every work block and report line opens by naming its root: his request with date, a standing instruction, or a plainly-stated reason. A root citing only machinery (alarm/gate/scheduled reminder) is not a root — must name the human instruction the machinery carries. Work whose root can't be named doesn't start; report line missing root is a defect. Home: "the grounded-work wish, ROADMAP row 569" — likely NOT in this file, but check.

TASK: Search the whole file (grep for "rule 1", "rule 2", "rule 5", "rule 25", "rule 29", "INV-28", "INV-35", "INV-69", "INV-83", "INV-137", "INV-152", "narrat", "contrast", "calque", "register-lint", "answer-first", "routing", "deferral", "root", "opus", "sonnet", "haiku", plus read the numbered rule list structure directly to find rules 1,2,5,25,29 and read their full text). For EACH of the 7 laws, report:
- Whether SKILL.md states it (full paraphrase/explanation) and where (exact line number range, e.g. "lines 140-158"), with a short quote (1 line) proving it's the real content not just a pointer.
- If found in multiple places (e.g. a summary list AND a detailed rule section), report each occurrence separately with line ranges.
- If NOT found (only a pointer/name, or absent entirely), say so explicitly per law.

Report back concisely: one section per law (1-7), each listing occurrences as "lines X-Y: <what it says, 1 quote>" or "not stated, pointer only" or "absent". Keep total report under 400 words plus the line citations.

3	description: Load before using any live-spec pack skill (spec-author, product-prover, design-reviewer, build-pipeline, test-author, communicator, feedback-intake, feedback-collector, text-audit, publish), before briefing a worker that will write files, or to resolve shared rules and settings. 6	---
7	
8	# live-spec-base — one rulebook, ten working skills
9	
10	The pack's shared working rules live here, once. A working skill opens by naming this base and the
11	version it was written against. It then references these rules and elaborates only its own domain.
12	The ten working skills are named in the closing roster below. A second full statement of a shared
13	rule inside a working skill is drift (SPEC INV-13). It is a defect to fold at the next milestone,
14	never kept for convenience. One rule is carried whole instead by every skill that briefs a worker.
15	The worker-restore sub-rule under rule 7 rides each brief in one wording. `tests/test_worker_restore.py`
16	reds a home that states it in words of its own (SPEC INV-299). Communicator teaches how to speak
17	plainly; that we speak plainly is this file's sentence. Used standalone, outside the pack, a
18	working skill still stands: its pointer here reads as plain advice.
19	
20	## Where the paths and the codes in this file point
21	
22	This file names paths of two kinds, resolving in two different trees.
23	
24	**The pack's own machinery** sits in the live-spec repository, whose public home is
25	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. Its directories are `guardrails/`, `scripts/`, `tests/`,
26	`templates/`, `hooks/`, `adopt/`, and `skills/`. Each of the ten working skills this file names sits
27	at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, beside this one.
28	
29	**A host's own documents and workspace** sit at the root of whatever project the pack is attached to.
30	Those are `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, `NEXT_STEPS.md`,
31	`DECISIONS.md`, `attic/`, `prototype/`, `inbox/`, `outbox/`, `docs/`, and `.live-spec/`. The live-spec
32	repository is a host of its own, so on that one machine the two trees are the same directory.
33	
34	A bracket code such as `INV-4` is a short handle for one rule of the product spec. Its home is
35	`PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, where the code trails the line it names. That file's preamble names every letter a
36	code can carry and what each stands for, so a code this page never uses decodes there. A roadmap row number, such as row 416, names a line of `ROADMAP.md`. A row that has closed
37	rotates to a dated file under `docs/queue-archive/`. So a row cited here may sit there instead. Two
38	other bracket marks read as part of the sentence they sit in, and `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` states both.
39	`[target]` marks a feature or leg that is promised and not yet built. `[default]` names a value the
40	agent set that the person may retune.
41	
42	## The words this file uses
43	
44	Each term is defined once. Most sit in the glossary of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, whose entry is the authority
45	behind the short read given here.
46	
47	- **the pack** — the shipped live-spec method: its skills, its document and suite templates, and its
48	  guardrail scripts. It carries a version.
49	- **a host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host holds its own spec, queue, journal, and
50	  `.live-spec/` folder.
51	- **the seat** — the one acting orchestrator session that owns judgment, orchestrates the pipeline,
52	  briefs workers, judges lane independence, and reports to the person. The glossary keeps the one name
53	  seat throughout. It records the senior and the orchestrator as the source's other names for it, and
54	  this file adds a fourth, the lead. The four names mean the one session.
55	- **a worker** — a delegated agent session the seat briefs for a bounded piece of mechanical work,
56	  narrowed to the files its brief names.
57	- **a tier** — the model level a unit of work runs at: a no-decision one-shot worker, a multi-step
58	  mechanical worker, or the seat for judgment. Rule 5 names haiku and sonnet as the two worker levels.
59	- **a brief** — the written instruction set a worker runs from, carrying its files, its steps, its
60	  clock, and its stop conditions.
61	- **a wish** — one request a person voices in plain words, captured as a queue row and carried to a
62	  recorded terminal state.
63	- **a queue row** — one live wish written as exactly five cells of `ROADMAP.md`: its id, the wish,
64	  its class, its status, and its acceptance. Its home is `docs/roadmap-format.md`. This file calls it
65	  a row.
66	- **a lane** — one build train a session rolls through the pipeline. A lane branch is that lane's
67	  isolated copy, a git worktree holding a branch named for its queue row.
68	- **the pen** — the single write-lock a repository holds, under which one delivery reaches the
69	  repository's shared truth at a time.
70	- **a landing** — the act of one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit
71	  under the pen.
72	- **a gate** — a check that must pass before work proceeds, and a red gate stops the work at that
73	  step. Where a sentence here says a check *reds* something, it means the check fails on it.
74	- **a checkpoint** — a saved point of work that can be resumed from, written under `.live-spec/`.
75	- **the attic** — the host's append-only archive folder `attic/`. A superseded file moves here with
76	  one manifest line and is kept for good.
77	- **a breakpoint** — a point where a movement ends and session memory can be wiped with no loss, its
78	  live state replaced, a dated journal entry added, and the work committed.
79	- **a door** — the intake classification placing a queued wish at one entry point of the pipeline,
80	  one of feature, bug, refactor, docs-only, or skip. An ask merely to see or try a thing takes a
81	  separate entry lane, the labelled-sketch door, held outside that five-way set.
82	- **an agent** — defined where the rule that binds it stands, at rule 31.
83	- **an agent card** — a host's self-describing file `.live-spec/agent.md`, stating its name, mission,
84	  zones, published contracts, and inbox address. `templates/agent.template.md` gives its shape.
85	
86	## The rule of thinking, above all the rest
87	
88	**Every incoming item is a symptom, and the answer owed is a rule about its class.** One phrase, one
89	file, one number, one incident — whatever arrives, it arrived as an instance of something. Name the
90	class, state the rule for it, find the other live instances, and the instance that was pointed at is
91	repaired as a free consequence. A change that repairs only the instance has answered nothing, because
92	the next instance is already on its way. The rule holds at every channel an item arrives through, and
93	there are three: a person's feedback, a finding the agent makes itself, and a message from another
94	agent. The three are one filter.
95	
96	This is a rule of thinking, and it governs every rule below it. Rule 14 is its mechanism inside a code
97	change. Rule 14 came first because the class-shaped answer was noticed in code, and the thinking
98	generalizes it to everything.
99	
100	Its own worked failure: the guard holding this pack's register laws was built as a list of literal
101	patterns. There was one pattern per phrase someone once caught. So the guard built to enforce the
102	rules was itself the clearest breach of this one. Each caught escape only added one more pattern,
103	while the next new phrasing passed through untouched (proven by probe, 2026-07-17). The repair
104	shipped that day as roadmap row 416, which now sits in
105	`docs/queue-archive/rotated-ROADMAP-2026-07.md`. A law naming a class is held by a judge that reads
106	meaning. If the answer to a class is a list, the design is wrong.
107	
108	## The shared rules
109	
110	Rule 30 was cut whole from this rulebook; its number is retired and stays open. Every other rule below
111	keeps the number it already carries.
112	
113	1. **Ask, never guess.** A gap only the human can fill — a threshold, a policy, a taste call — is asked or
114	   marked `⟨DECIDE⟩` with a one-line question and a recommended pick. Never invent intent, and never ask
115	   what you can decide or verify yourself. A pending question rides in its row while the lane keeps moving
116	   on the recommendation (SPEC INV-4, INV-5, INV-12). And before offering the human a fork, check whether
117	   a proven artifact already settles it. Where the architecture, the spec, or the invariants determine
118	   the answer, derive the requirement. Say it back with the section cited as its ground, offering no fork.
119	   A fork reaches the human only for what the artifacts leave genuinely open (rule 27 names those cases).
120	   This is the read-the-doc twin of ask-never-guess: that half forbids inventing an answer, this half
121	   forbids offering a choice the documents have already made (SPEC INV-121).
122	
123	2. **Plain words carry the meaning; the code trails, quietly.** Every human-facing sentence stands on its
124	   own in the product's language. Internal handles never do the talking: an `INV-x` code, a row number, a
125	   worker name, a model name, a coined feature name, or a metaphor the reader never chose to learn.
126	   One convention, two faces: in **chat**, the anchor may trail the sentence in parentheses —
127	   "no remote copy exists (INV-8)"; in **documents**, anchors sit at line ends in square brackets — `[INV-8]`.
128	   Never open a line with a code. And when chat runs in one language while the docs run in another, a term
129	   or metaphor coined in the docs language is never loan-translated into chat. That is the **no calques**
130	   rule: say what actually happens in natural chat-language words. The original term is free to trail in parentheses like any
131	   anchor. (2026-07-05 — a calque reads as machine-speak and degrades the product.)
132	
133	3. **One surface = one name, everywhere.** The moment one thing answers to two names, every cross-check
134	   silently loses the seam between them. The vocabulary comes from the host's SPEC.
135	
136	4. **One canonical home per fact.** Everything else that mentions the fact is a pointer, and pointers are
137	   kept live — a doc superseded or moved gets every inbound reference repointed the same session. Two
138	   documents claiming authority over one fact is undefined behaviour when they disagree.
139	
140	5. **The lead orchestrates; each unit routes to the cheapest tier that passes its brief (SPEC INV-69).**
141	   The lead — the orchestrator seat, whatever tier holds it — orchestrates, briefs, and accepts the work,
142	   and it does not do the grunt itself. Every unit of work is routed PER UNIT:
143	   the trigger is judgment against mechanical, and the tier is proposed for that unit. A one-shot with no
144	   decision goes to haiku, multi-step mechanical work to sonnet, and anything carrying judgment or design
145	   to the senior, and a judgment step is never routed down. Size is a weak hint only, never the decider.
146	   The worker pastes raw output (command + exit code + failing lines) as it works. Only raw output is
147	   evidence, and the worker's prose is only a lead. So a worker's green is a lead the lead ACCEPTS by
148	   re-checking it, never on trust. A
149	   large or high-stakes landing earns an independent fresh-context checker beyond that re-check (SPEC
150	   INV-46). Every override of a proposed tier and every
151	   failed-acceptance escalation is logged, proposed tier → chosen tier → why (SPEC INV-69).
152	
153	6. **Every long or delegated piece of work keeps a persistent checkpoint.** A file on disk (host home:
154	   `.live-spec/checkpoints/`, gitignored and kept inside the repo tree) holds done / in-progress / next,
155	   updated as the work runs, so a cut-off resumes from disk. A landing that ships a checkpoint's items flips that checkpoint to its closed state in the same
156	   landing, so a returning session never reopens finished work. A checkpoint whose items all live in git
157	   history is stale by definition and reads as a resume defect (SPEC INV-107). Red at a pause is never
158	   committed. The failing test name and the hypothesis become the top item of `NEXT_STEPS.md`, so the
159	   red test is itself the checkpoint. A checkpoint or handoff note that records a live background
160	   worker also records three things about it. First, the worker's id, pointing at the worker's own
161	   checkpoint file. Second, its briefed write-set. Third, the liveness checks a resuming session runs
162	   before touching those files or spawning a sibling. Those checks are the write-set's file times
163	   watched over a short window, the worker's heartbeat, and one message to its id. The heartbeat is a
164	   fixed-interval touch on the worker's own checkpoint file, ~60 s [default],
165	   stale past ~2 min [default]. Such a note never frames the worker's output as finished while the
166	   worker may still run (SPEC INV-76). Before a memory wipe, prefer
167	   halting the workers or letting them finish, so the next session starts single-writer. Say plainly
168	   when a worker dies with a closed window or a sleeping machine. The human's leave-word fires this rule
169	   for everything open at once. Every lane goes to its checkpoint, workers are halted or landed, and green
170	   is committed. One closing line follows, only when the whole walk holds (SPEC INV-95; the communicator
171	   carries the walk).
172	
173	7. **The concurrent-edit fence, before every write and every commit.** Re-check `git status` and HEAD
174	   against what you last read. If HEAD moved, or the tree holds changes you did not make, stop, re-read,
175	   then proceed surgically or back off. A repo you were not assigned to is read-only, apart from a new wish
176	   file in its inbox. This binds every skill that writes shared files, adoption among them (SPEC INV-10,
177	   INV-11).
178	
179	   The parallel-lanes rules sit underneath the fence.
180	   - **Lanes under one pen, up to the profile cap.** Within one session, build lanes roll without asking up
181	     to the profile-declared lane cap (SPEC T-18; `lanes.cap`, package default three [E-13]). One more
182	     opens only on the human's asked word. Every write to a document the lanes share serializes under the
183	     single PEN, one lane at a time. That document is a convergence point the pen reconciles at
184	     integration, so sharing it never makes the lanes wait on each other. Co-location alone never pulls two rows into one lane (SPEC INV-49).
185	   - **The lane-open act.** The session opens a lane by running `scripts/open-lane.sh`, or by walking the
186	     same steps by hand. The script's own header states what it expects on disk. First, the row→in-work flip is committed to main under the pen. Second, the branch
187	     `lane/<row>-<slug>` is cut from that claim commit into its own worktree. Third, the lane goes to a
188	     worker whose brief names the branch. The act reads the profile cap [E-13] and refuses a lane past it.
189	     It runs whenever the dependency graph shows two or more independent runnable rows and lanes stand free.
190	     Going single-file then is recorded on the departures board, the status-report view, as a "serial by the
191	     graph" board reason. Judging independence is a senior read no gate can settle, so this stays a
192	     discipline the session holds (SPEC INV-214, INV-49).
193	   - **Worktree isolation on overlap.** A later lane's code and tests live in its own isolated copy of the
194	     tree until the senior integrates them. So worktree isolation is the default when two lanes' write-sets
195	     overlap. A shared file one lane holds open is never written by another (SPEC INV-105).
196	   - **Brief-time disjointness** — before spawning another concurrent writer, the senior confirms its
197	     brief's write-set is disjoint from every already-running writer's brief, or gives it an isolated
198	     worktree at brief-time. The fence stays silent between same-session siblings and cannot catch the
199	     senior's own workers colliding (SPEC ACT-3, INV-11).
200	   - **A worker never restores a working tree with a git command (SPEC INV-298).** Before a worker mutates a file it means to put back, it reads that file and holds its bytes. A worker puts a file back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED BYTES. A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any tree: `git checkout -- <path>`, `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and `git clean` with `-f` or `-x`. 526	     producer's tree on the owner's explicit permission, recorded with its date and its author. How a
527	     neighbour's product happens to be built grants no permission, and a field with no recorded
528	     permission stays home. Credentials never cross under any permission [INV-185].
529	   - **An agent recognises a neighbour's zone on its own.** An agent may meet a fault or a lack in something
530	     another agent's zone owns: a rule of the method, a shape a neighbour ships, a field a contract
531	     lacks. It then scans for cards, finds the owner, and takes the channel that fits. The owner
532	     naming the road afterwards carries no fact the agent lacked, so his line is an acknowledgement of a
533	     thing already done. An agent that waits to be told has made the owner its router [INV-195].
534	   - **One question crosses between two agents twice, and the third crossing goes to the owner.** Every
535	     hop of a refer-and-re-send loop can pass its own law while the exchange manufactures traffic, so the
536	     bound is two, counted by the exchange's identifier. The third crossing is named in the sender's own
537	     status report as a zone question the two could not settle. The human-decision withdrawal loop
538	     already takes this shape [INV-196, INV-130].
539	   - **A concern no agent's zone owns goes to the pack, and the work never stalls on ownership.** A
540	     question no work stands on is dropped [INV-191]. A concern is a different thing: real work whose
541	     owning zone does not exist yet. It goes to the pack's inbox, and the pack answers who owns it — an
542	     existing agent, a new agent the owner ratifies, or a skill. Zones may overlap and no agent is
543	     forced to carve a disjoint one. The work never waits on the answer. An agent meeting an unowned
544	     concern does the reasonable thing now, in whatever tree can hold it, and marks that work
545	     provisional. The re-home lands later as ordinary pipeline work, cheap and retroactive, where a stall
546	     while ownership is settled is what this rule prevents [INV-197].
547	   - **A capability another agent's zone owns is taken through one of the two channels.** Building
548	     a local copy of a neighbour's capability is the violation the cards exist to prevent. The
549	     copy drifts from its original the day after it is made, and the two owners then answer one question
550	     two ways [INV-194]. An agent-initiated message stays a proposal until the owner ratifies it. An
551	     owner-initiated message is the one kind that carries the owner's authority, and relaying changes a
552	     message's carrier while leaving its authority where it started [INV-193].
553	
554	32. **A release's number answers what taking it costs a host (SPEC INV-217).** The number reports what a
555	   host that vendored the previous version must do to take this one. A **patch** fixes a machine to hold a
556	   law already stated: no new capability, no changed contract, and the host takes it and does nothing. A
557	   **minor** grows what a host may adopt in a backward-compatible way: a new capability, a new law, or a
558	   new gate. The host takes it by re-running its catch-up walk [INV-91], with nothing it already carries
559	   rewritten. A **major** is a release a host cannot take without changing what it already carries. Four
560	   things earn it: a reworded rule the host vendored, a renamed or removed surface a host depends on, a
561	   changed adoption or catch-up step, a moved law that forces host action. A major ships its dated
562	   `MIGRATION.md` chapter [INV-91]. The default is a patch. It is raised to a minor or a major only where
563	   the release earns the higher tier. This is a judgment the releasing session makes and states, **held by
564	   no machine**. The minor-versus-major call reads meaning a gate cannot, so it **stays a stated rule the
565	   session holds**, the same standing as a design-review finding that never blocks a lane [INV-141]. The
566	   2.0.0 release is the boundary case. Its migration chapter records "Host action: none", so by this rule
567	   it reads as a minor. It keeps its published number as this cited boundary case.
568	
569	33. **The authoring seat does not adversarially certify its own work (SPEC INV-237).** The seat that
570	   authored a change drafts and accepts it, and it never provides that change's own adversarial
571	   certification. A head marinated in the authoring context is blind to the blind spot it just wrote. Two
572	   carriers hold it. A release's adversarial pass — the full re-prove at the release gate [INV-116] — is
573	   authored by a fresh seat. That seat is a differently-contexted head briefed from the primary sources.
574	   It is the same freshness the verify audit already demands of its checker (SPEC INV-46).
575	   The 2.7.0 release ran its adversarial pass
576	   in the context that authored the new lenses, and so
577	   never turned a brand-new lens onto the skill body that introduced it. And a newly added lens or rule is
578	   run against the very document that introduces it before release, which is self-application, with the
579	   release record
580	   naming the result. A release gate may require a dated clean-context review record naming a seat other
581	   than the release's. Whether the review was truly clean-context is a process fact no gate fully sees.
582	   So the gate checks only that the record exists, is dated to the release, and names a different seat.
583	   That is the mechanical floor under a discipline the seat holds. The owner's word, 2026-07-18, after a fresh web
584	   review caught self-referential defects the in-context 2.7.0 prover missed.
585	
586	34. **A deferred item's own state is re-derived from the code before its work resumes (SPEC INV-247).** A
587	   resume file and a queue row record a past moment. The technical problem statement a deferred or
588	   queued item carries — how the code it touches works — can go stale as that code moves on. So the first
589	   act of resuming such an item is a freshness check of its own subject against the shipped source. Read
590	   the code the item touches, confirm the problem the row describes still holds, and re-derive the item's
591	   real current state before designing anything on it. It is the resume-side twin of rule 13's primary
592	   source and of the architecture step's pin read from a command just run. Rule 8 re-reads versions at a
593	   breakpoint, and the queue-take re-scan re-reads a deferred row's revisit trigger [SPEC INV-129].
594	   This rule re-reads the item's own internals. So
595	   a session never designs a fix from a stale model of code that has since moved, and an item already handled
596	   is caught before the work restarts. The owner asked the pack to hold it, 2026-07-20.
597	
598	35. **A session's record is read at both ends by an agent that did not live it (SPEC INV-302).** A session
599	   that lived the work reads its own record badly. Worked failure: on 2026-07-28 a session wrote its
600	   handover from memory. It named a question as still waiting for the owner, and the owner had answered
601	   it earlier that day. So each
602	   end of a session is read by a fresh agent. That agent works from a session extract: the person's own
603	   turns, each with its timestamp. `scripts/session-extract.py` pulls those turns out of one transcript,
604	   and its own header names where the transcripts sit and which traps a reader meets there.
605	   The extract goes to a scratch directory, since a transcript holds private conversation. At the close,
606	   the fresh agent writes the session handover from that extract. The session that lived the work writes
607	   no handover of its own. A handover is a file under `docs/handovers/` whose name ends in
608	   `-handover.md`, and it says where it was read from in three lines: transcript, extract, written by.
609	   At the open, a fresh agent reads the previous session's extract. It lists every decision the person
610	   made, each with its timestamp. It compares that list against `DECISIONS.md` and `NEXT_STEPS.md`. A
611	   decision missing from both goes to the seat before work starts.
612	   Both ends stay a discipline the seat holds. A script read the handover's three lines until
613	   2026-08-09, and the live-spec pack withdrew that script after finding no error the script had
614	   ever caught.
615	   A session's opening writes no committed artifact for a script to read. The owner asked for
616	   this reading as a standing process, 2026-07-28.
617	
618	
619	## Work that belongs elsewhere
620	
621	Reserve this file for the pack's own work: a session outside the pack uses a general style guide instead.
622	Never write host- or person-specific values here — those live in profiles, and this file holds only
623	package defaults and the rules themselves. The scope is pack-internal by the owner's decision (recorded
624	2026-07-16). The base serves the pack's skills and the projects that adopted the pack. It is no
625	general-purpose rulebook for unrelated sessions. That decided sentence closes the recurring scope
626	question for good.
627	
628	## The settings ladder
629	
630	How the pack behaves is a **named setting** living in one of four nested scopes, and a setting belongs to
631	the scope it describes. Broader values are inherited downward until a narrower scope overrides them on
632	the human's word. Resolution reads from the narrowest scope out — **session beats host beats personal beats
633	package default** (SPEC E-13):
634	
635	| Scope | Home | Holds settings about |
636	|---|---|---|
637	| package defaults | the table below, in this file | the pack out of the box |
638	| personal profile | `~/.claude/live-spec/profile.md` | the person — follows them across every project |
639	| host profile | `<host>/.live-spec/profile.md` | this one project |
640	| session | the human's live word, held only in the conversation itself | the conversation running right now |
641	
642	An override exists only as a written line in its profile file. Setting one leaves a dated journal note
643	in the home it governs, keeping every divergence visible (SPEC INV-14). The session scope is the one exception.
644	It lives only in the human's spoken word and dies with the conversation. The agent never writes it
645	anywhere on its own. Making it outlive the session is a promotion into the profile it describes, on
646	the human's word, journaled like any other override. Proactivity mode and trust are written
647	only on the human's word, and the agent may propose but never set them (SPEC INV-9). Profiles are re-read at the same
648	freshness points as skills (rule 8). A profile line the current pack does not recognize is ignored out
649	loud, named once in the session's next report as a visible, ordinary skip, never an error.
650	
651	**The profile is found or founded at setup (SPEC B-3)**. The pack looks for the personal profile before
652	the founding questions resolve. It looks at founding, at adoption's orient, and at the first session on
653	a new machine or with a new human. Found ⇒ loaded and said aloud. Absent ⇒ an offer to create it from
654	`templates/profile.template.md`, which sits in the pack's own tree. The human tells about themselves and
655	may name sources for the pack to read and propose from. Every line lands on the human's word, and a declined proposal is dropped (INV-9
656	caps it: mode and trust move only on their word). A declined step runs the session on package
657	defaults, said aloud, and the offer returns at the next setup. A worker session never onboards
658	anyone, since its brief carries its setting lines (SPEC ACT-3).
659	
660	The personal layer has one home, the profile. The machine-global instruction file (for example
661	`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) is a thin loader. It carries the pointer that loads the profile, plus only the
662	bootstrap lines that must hold before
663	any pack file is read. It is those bootstrap lines' one home, and the profile never restates them (SPEC E-16).
664	
665	### Package defaults
666	
667	| Setting | Default | A profile may say | Card |
668	|---|---|---|---|
669	| `language.docs` | English — docs, commits, code, artifacts | another docs language | visible |
670	| `language.chat` | mirror the human's language | pin one (e.g. Russian) | visible |
671	| `proactivity.mode` | ask-at-max — surface forks, wait on taste calls | max-proactive: proceed on recommendations, batch questions | visible |
672	| `trust` | low — human word before outward moves | raised only by the human (INV-9) | internal |
673	| `prover.cadence` | FULL pass before every MINOR bump; CROSS-LINK on every surface add | tighter (e.g. live-spec itself: before every push) or looser, recorded | internal |
674	| `worker.tiering` | router proposes the cheapest sufficient tier; senior may override, logged | fixed tier per size class (SPEC D-2) | internal |
675	| `checkpoints.home` | `<host>/.live-spec/checkpoints/`, gitignored | another host path | internal |
676	| `spec.file` | `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` — the host's product spec file; every pack guide reads "PRODUCT_SPEC.md" as this file under its recorded name | a host that adopted under its own name keeps it, recorded as one host-profile line (e.g. `spec.file: SPEC.md`); a rename may be offered together with its pointer sweep, never forced (SPEC INV-90) | internal |
677	| `work-kind.host-default` | none — each wish's kind is called at intake | a host with one usual kind names it as the intake default (SPEC T-16) | internal |
678	| `project.kind` | none — asked at founding and at adoption's orient, always the human's answer, never profile-seeded or inferred (SPEC INV-36) | the host's own kind: book · backend service · static site · fullstack app · CLI · skill pack · a custom kind through the queue; seeds project-wide defaults, never overriding an explicit line; updated on the human's word the moment the project outgrows it, journaled | visible |
679	| `project.layers` | none — declared at founding beside `project.kind`, naming this kind's concrete footprint categories (SPEC INV-135) | this project's own categories, one line: a codebase's frontend/backend/store, a photo site's content/rendering-engine/deployment, a campaign's message/channels/assets; the per-kind footprint-and-proof table in `ARCHITECTURE.md` is the scaffold each founding fills | internal |
680	| `project.proofs` | none — declared at founding beside `project.kind`, naming this kind's concrete test-ladder rungs (SPEC INV-135) | this project's own rungs, one line: tests and rendered checks, a byte-diff and an eye-walk, a register lint and the owner's review; a `project.kind` recorded with neither layers nor proofs is incomplete | internal |
681	| `project.design-principles` | none for a kind with no visual surface; a visual kind (e.g. frontend / fullstack app) declares its set at founding, seeded from that kind's starter table in `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s per-kind design-principles section (SPEC INV-136) | the project's own checkable design rules, one line, extended past the starter set through the queue; a visual kind recorded with none is flagged the way a kind recorded with no layers or proofs is (SPEC INV-135) | internal |
682	| `design-sync` | off — a host with visual components may switch it on (recorded profile line, SPEC E-18, INV-14) | on: a landing's declared components sync to the team's design project, every sync behind the human's publish gate (rule 17) | internal |
683	| `feedback-upstream` | off — the outbound feedback arm is silent; a host switches it on with a recorded profile line (SPEC INV-161, INV-14) | on: on a rare strong reaction the pack offers, with the human's explicit yes, to draft a private upstream note to the pack's authors into `outbox/`; never sends, delivery the human's own step | internal |
684	| `lanes.cap` | 3 — up to three build lanes roll at once without asking (SPEC T-18, INV-214) | a leaner plan lowers it, a richer one raises it, recorded with the plan it fits; the owner's 2026-07-06 value of three lives in his profile | internal |
685	| `budget.pressure` | full — every check runs at full strength; the economy ladder's rung (SPEC T-19, INV-40); a rung moves the pace and never the standard, stated under this table | lean or tight, only on the human's word (a session's word or a profile line; asked — or the default told — at a project's setup, founding or adoption, alongside `project.kind`; the agent proposes a rung when money/time pressure is named, never sets one); each rung's legal sheds and the never-bend list live in the economy-ladder section of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` — every taken shed is named in the delivery report, and an explicit host line outlives any rung | visible |
686	| `far-tier.surface-cadence` | at most once every 14 days — how often the far backlog may surface itself unasked in the status report (SPEC INV-223, roadmap row 403); the report records the last surfacing in a dated marker, and a second offer inside the window is the defect the report-shape check reds | the person's own cadence, moved by his word like any default, and recorded in his profile | internal |
687	
688	The Card column says what the settings card renders. A `visible` row appears on the card. An `internal` row is workshop machinery the card leaves out, reaching the reader only as a recorded host-profile line in the card's project-rules part. The card's own law lives in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (INV-87).
689	
690	A profile file is plain markdown: one `setting: value` line per override, each with a trailing date and,
691	when it narrows the defaults, one line saying why. Settings not listed above may be proposed as wishes, and the
692	table grows through the queue like everything else.
693	
694	### A budget moves the pace, and never the standard
695	
696	A rung of the economy ladder sets how fast and how cheaply the work runs. The standard the work is held
697	to stands outside every rung. A check the method calls for runs at whatever the plan costs. A fresh
698	clean-context agent is raised every time the method asks for one. Four such asks are an adversarial
699	review, a cold reading, a release re-prove, and a deep spec-and-architecture audit. Economy is bought
700	from pace, from batching, and from a cheaper tier on mechanical work. It is never bought from a
701	dropped check. The full never-bend list this rule joins lives in the economy-ladder section of
702	`PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (SPEC INV-40, R220). The owner's word, 2026-08-05 at 22:52: quality never suffers,
703	whatever else does. At 22:12 he had named the smaller plan. He asked that a fresh worker the method
704	needs be raised on it all the same.
705	
706	> The pack, whole: **live-spec-base** holds the shared rules and defaults · **spec-author** writes the spec ·
707	> **product-prover** reviews it · **product-prover-pack** binds the external prover to the pack · **design-reviewer** judges the design behind it · **build-pipeline** ships the change · **test-author** derives the matrix and writes the tests · **communicator** makes the human
708	> exchange land · **feedback-intake** brings what comes back to its home · **feedback-collector** offers a rare private note up to the authors · **text-audit** reads a text as a stranger and fixes where they stop · **publish** sees the work out the door, owing its kind's checklist.
